rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's threat against the idols and monotheistic message were public and emphatic; people dismissed them as youthful passion and assumed he would never attack the idols, so after the event they identified him by his known criticism.
rows.anchor: The threat sounded by Abraham (sws) regarding the idols was done in an emphatic way and before people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling him a youngster named Abraham suggests he was not personally famous, though his name circulated and he was known in some circles for rebellious opposition to ancestral religion.
rows.anchor: his name had reached various circles and he was beginning to be known as someone who had rebellious tendencies against their ancestral religion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chiefs summoned Abraham publicly so everyone would see the inquiry into what they considered a grave offense and its stern punishment; religious chiefs issued such verdicts, with government only implementing them.
rows.anchor: Once Abraham (sws) had been accused of this move against their idols, he was summoned in public by the chiefs of his nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's answer in the public proceeding cornered the elders and forced their defeat; their response is depicted in verses 65–66.
rows.anchor: completely cornered the elders of his nation and they were not left with anything but to confess defeat.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some readers take Abraham's answer as fearful, but Islahi says his public proclamation of monotheism and open threat against the idols make that reading illogical.
rows.anchor: then right in the middle of the court proceedings cursed the idols and their worshippers by the words “shame on you”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the view that Abraham's answer was a lie, Islahi reads it as deliberate sarcasm, meaningful mockery, and staged argument; its wording does not indicate falsehood.
rows.anchor: What can be said about it is that his words constituted a very subtle form of sarcasm, meaningful mockery and a gradual sequence of argumentation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi argues that Abraham's own opponents never accused him of lying despite having ample opportunity, so later readers should not call him a liar.
rows.anchor: his own people never even accused him of lying. They could have easily done so if they really thought that he was lying.

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some people cite a hadith that Abraham lied three times and count this answer as one of them; Islahi says they have misunderstood the hadith.
rows.anchor: Some people were led to form this view because of a ḥadīth in which it is stated that Abraham had lied three times.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic word kadhib can mean lying, making a mistake, or using a double meaning; context determines which sense is intended.
rows.anchor: just as it means “he lied” it also means “he made a mistake” as well “he implied a double-meaning.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A double-meaning statement can lead an opponent to misunderstand the speaker's intent; Abraham's gradual argument is an instance of this device.
rows.anchor: what is said before one’s rival makes him misunderstand what the speaker intends to convey.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says subtle, well-intended double meanings occur in the Qur'an and early authorities' speech, including Joseph's story and Abraham's “I am ill” at 37:89; this device is sound and can serve the righteous effectively.
rows.anchor: such double-meaning statements are found in the Qur’ān and also in the conversations of our illustrious predecessors of the past.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's act refutes polytheism: if several deities govern, the chief has no reason to accept partners, or could later dismantle their partnership; his audience understood the lesson but could not accept it.
rows.anchor: there is no reason for the chief deity to accept others as his partners.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's action startled the people and briefly returned them to innate guidance: they recognized that they were the wrongdoers, since their deities could neither ward off harm nor speak up.
rows.anchor: The verse implies that this measure undertaken by Abraham (sws) did startle them and they did turn towards their innate guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word nakasa means to topple something onto its head, describing the people's heads dropping after their brief recognition.
rows.anchor: means to topple something on its head. In other words, they did open their eyes for a while

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People may briefly see truth after a warning, but bias prevents acceptance; they become deaf and blind again and return to their old ways.
rows.anchor: their bias and prejudice does not let them accept the truth. As a result, they again become deaf and blind and revert to their ill-ways.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the people admitted the idols' inability to speak, Abraham's question about worshipping powerless beings landed forcefully because their helplessness was already evident.
rows.anchor: They could only have had the required impact after the helplessness of the idols had become evident.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression translated “shame on you” conveys intense hatred and aversion; Abraham says it after fully communicating the truth and leaving his people no excuse.
rows.anchor: extreme hate and aversion. It was uttered once Abraham (sws) had conclusively communicated the truth to his people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concluding question exposes the foolishness of worshipping stone idols that cannot defend or help themselves.
rows.anchor: themselves? How can help them?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once the idol worshippers and temple priests felt exposed, they rallied the masses and considered proposals for dealing with Abraham; the priests judged burning him the most effective response.
rows.anchor: they opined that burning him would be the most effective measure.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an does not explain how God protected Abraham from the fire; Islahi says nature's effects remain under God's control, so removing fire's effect is possible, as with poison and other extraordinary events.
rows.anchor: all elements of nature are under God’s control and hence if the fire was deprived of its effects

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The priests' failed plot to burn Abraham is also mentioned at 37:98; after it failed, Abraham migrated.
rows.anchor: also refers to it. There I will, God willing, explain it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessed land is Canaan; when Abraham could no longer remain in his homeland, God rescued him and Lot from their peoples and took them there.
rows.anchor: The land referred to here is Canaan. In other words, when matters reached the extent that Abraham (sws) could not stay in his country

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot was Abraham's nephew; their preaching circles differed, but both accompanied each other on the migration and preached to their respective peoples until leaving, then settled in separate regions.
rows.anchor: Lot (sws) was Abraham’s nephew. Even though the circle of preaching of both was different, both accompanied each other in this migration.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says it is unknown what happened to Abraham's people after he left them.
rows.anchor: people after he left them is not known.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Abraham left family and kin for God's sake, God compensated him with sons, grandsons, and pious descendants in place of his wretched relatives.
rows.anchor: These verses mention the favours God blessed Abraham (sws) with one after the other after he had migrated.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says Ishmael came in response to Abraham's supplication, while Isaac, Jacob, and later prophets were additional gifts; he refers to 21:100–112 and says Farāhī exposed a Jewish distortion of this history.
rows.anchor: God granted Ishmael (sws) to Abraham (sws) as a result of his supplication, He also blessed him in addition with Isaac (sws) and Jacob (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophets were founders and leaders of nations; although every prophet is a leader by status, some had no followers, while Isaac and Jacob were appointed leaders of their people.
rows.anchor: Both Isaac (sws) and Jacob (sws) were in fact leaders of their nation and appointed by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase iqāmat al-ṣalāh is transposed in the verse, with the tāʾ marbūṭa dropped to preserve its beat and rhythm; such elision is common in Arabic.
rows.anchor: been dropped in deference to the beat and rhythm of the verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning these prophets' worship, prayer, and zakāh shows their message matched the Qur'an: they worshipped God alone; people claiming their legacy should measure how far their beliefs and deeds have strayed.
rows.anchor: By pointing out the components of the message of these prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage shifts from Lot's appearance alongside Abraham to a separate discussion of Lot.
rows.anchor: Earlier Lot (sws) was mentioned
